narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 68% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. While the average student who is accepted ranks around the 6th decile, you placed in the 3rd decile, signaling consistently weaker academic performance relative to your peers. This was the single biggest reason the model doubted your likelihood of passing the bar.

Your LSAT score was the second most important factor and also pulled the prediction toward failure. At 18, your score sits far below the average of 37 seen among accepted applicants, giving the model further reason to expect difficulty with the bar exam.

Your undergraduate GPA was the third most influential feature, but it worked in the opposite direction. At 3.20, it is only slightly below the 3.23 average of accepted students. This gave the model a small positive signal that you could still succeed, yet it was not enough to overcome the negative impact of your class rank and LSAT.

Taken together, these academic signals led the model to conclude you are more likely than not to fail the bar on the first try. To improve your chances, you should focus on raising your LSAT score significantly through intensive preparation, consider repeating key coursework to strengthen your class rank, and then reapply. This targeted effort on your weakest areas can meaningfully change future predictions. (248 words)
